title: Shelfburst latency vs dollar comparison - draft
content:
Overview:
This is a working brief comparing two production knobs for handling short-lived "shelf" bursts: synchronous small-session fast-path (SP) vs shelf-multiplex (SM) on a 4xA100 node pool. The aim is to show latency percentile tradeoffs and amortized $/query under a realistic micro-interaction workload (median request 12 tokens out, short-lived sessions).

Experiment summary:
- Model: open-llm-mini-13B quantized to 8-bit (baseline) and 4-bit compact (opt)
- Nodes: 4x A100-80GB per pool, batcher configured with 20ms batching window for SP and 80ms opportunistic window for SM
- Workload: synthetic micro-interactions trace (40k sessions, Poisson arrival, peak 400 qps sustained for 30s bursts every 3m)
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), tail jitter (ms stdev), QPS per GPU, amortized $/1M queries (using current infra ratecard)
- Notes: KV cache hit simulated at 18% (session affinity preserved for 60s)

ASCII charts (median trial, aggregated across 3 runs):

Latency percentiles (ms):
Scenario      | p50  | p95  | p99  | p99.9
--------------|------|------|------|-------
FastPath (SP) | 22   | 110  | 320  | 540   
ShelfMux (SM) | 45   | 160  | 420  | 610   

Observations: SP gives much lower median and mid-percentile latency but has a heavier tail when many concurrent micro-sessions contend for slots (p99 delta ~100ms vs SM). SM smooths tails by absorbing into multiplex slots but increases median by ~20-25ms.

Tail jitter (p99-p95) across time window (ms):
- SP: mean=210, stdev=75
- SM: mean=260, stdev=40
Interpretation: SP exhibits more bursty tail spikes (higher stdev) while SM is more consistent but elevated.

Throughput and slot efficiency:
- SP: average 0.9 QPS/GPU during bursts (lower packing), but higher per-interaction slot reservation overhead
- SM: average 1.6 QPS/GPU during same period (better packing), fewer wasted slots at expense of slightly higher per-request latency

Cost arithmetic (back-of-envelope using current infra rates):
- Assumptions: A100 pool cost = $3.20/hour per GPU equivalent (blended infra), hourly amortization + platform overhead = 1.35x multiplier to compute per-GPU effective cost.
- Effective cost per GPU-hour = $4.32
- Queries per GPU-hour during burst (observed): SP=3,240 QPH, SM=5,760 QPH
- $/1M queries = (GPU-hour cost * hours per million queries)
  * SP: 1M / 3,240 = 308.6 GPU-hours => 308.6 * $4.32 = $1,334.7 per 1M queries
  * SM: 1M / 5,760 = 173.6 GPU-hours => 173.6 * $4.32 = $749.1 per 1M queries

Qualitative tradeoffs:
- SP: best for latency-sensitive micros (median/p50-critical paths), useful where perceived latency dominates user satisfaction (chat UI quick replies). Heavy tails and lower packing reduce cost efficiency.
- SM: best for cost-sensitive high-throughput micros where p95 is acceptable within the 150-200ms range. Better slot utilization reduces $/query materially.

Micro-chart: latency vs cost frontier (text):
- Point A (SP + 8-bit): p95=110ms, $/1M=1335
- Point B (SM + 8-bit): p95=160ms, $/1M=749
- Point C (SP + 4-bit): p95=95ms, $/1M=980 (quantization helps both latency and cost for SP)
- Point D (SM + 4-bit): p95=140ms, $/1M=560

Actionable knobs tested and immediate recommendations:
1) For tiers with strict p50 SLAs (internal fast-product tier), enable SP with prewarm=2 slots + 4-bit quantization. Expected outcome: p50 ~18ms, p95 ~95ms, $/1M drop ~27% vs SP+8-bit.
2) For default free-tier / high-volume customer flows: enable SM with aggressive opportunistic window (60-100ms) + 4-bit quantization + aggressive slot packing. Expected outcome: ~45% cost reduction vs SP baseline with acceptable p95 for UI flows.
3) Adaptive routing: implement a simple heuristic in the router to pick SP for requests with "interactive:true" header and SM otherwise. Route sampling to verify regression risk.

Open questions / TODOs:
- We simulated KV hit at 18% — need to re-run with real session affinity traces from prod (INF-4912) to validate hit sensitivity.
- Evaluate memory pressure for 4-bit models in long burst windows — run soak test @ 24 hours.
- Measure client-side tail (network + TLS) to isolate infra vs app jitter — add p50/p99 breakdown in next run.
- Cost model currently omits storage/network egress for embeddings-heavy flows; re-evaluate for multimodal experiments.

Appendix: quick run config snippets (notes to self):
- SP: batch_window_ms=20, concurrency_slots=4, prewarm=2, quant_profile=4bit-fast
- SM: batch_window_ms=80, multiplex_slots=12, multiplex_timeout_ms=120, quant_profile=4bit-compact

Relevant links / tickets:
- JIRA INF-4821: shelfburst benchmark harness
- GH PR: github.com/redwood-inference/fastpath/pull/2023 (mux scheduler changes)
- Confluence: performance/shelfburst-brief (working landing)

Draft conclusions (for discussion):
- ShelfMux (SM) is a strong cost-win for high-volume micro-interactions and should be the default for non-latency-critical traffic.
- FastPath (SP) remains necessary for top-tier latency promises; pair with 4-bit quantization and prewarm to contain tails.
- Next step: ship routing sampler + 24hr soak run with real session traces, then present results in Eng Ops sync.

Notes to reviewers: this doc is a working brief; figures are from synthetic harness and rounded. Please add comments inline, flag if we should pivot to a multi-model comparison (we only tested one model here).
